query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Utilizing an in situ measurement method combining high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction with environmental TEM will enable simultaneous real‐time observation of oxidation scale growth and phase transformations in advanced high-temperature alloys, providing a more accurate assessment of oxidation kinetics and phase stability.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-homogenized high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi HEA) with a single-phase solid solution structure.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to high-temperature conditions in an oxidizing atmosphere while performing simultaneous in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction and environmental TEM imaging.
generation.conditions: Temperatures ranging from approximately 800°C to 1200°C under a controlled oxidizing environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolving oxide scale on the surface and the underlying crystallographic phase structure of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The simultaneous measurement approach captures the kinetics of oxide scale formation via XRD (by monitoring diffraction peak shifts and emergence of new phases) and concurrently images microstructural changes using TEM, thereby linking oxidation behaviour to phase transformations.
generation.predicted_outcome: The combined in situ approach will resolve time–temperature-dependent growth of oxide scales and phase transformations; for instance, as the oxidation scale thickens, a correlated shift or transformation in the underlying phase structure (e.g., modifications in peak intensities or emergence/disappearance of diffraction peaks) is expected.
generation.baseline: Independent measurements of oxidation (using only high-temperature XRD) or phase transformations (using stand-alone TEM) in similar alloys under comparable conditions.
generation.boundary: This method may be limited by temporal or spatial resolution constraints, particularly for ultra-rapid transformations or nanoscale phenomena in alloys with extremely fine microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: While the method is expected to capture simultaneous oxidation and phase change phenomena, the precise quantitative correlation between oxide scale growth and phase transformation kinetics may vary with alloy composition, temperature gradients, and instrument resolution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of high-entropy alloy samples with known high-temperature oxidation and phase transformation behaviours. Subject one set to traditional stand-alone high-temperature XRD measurements and another set to the combined in situ synchrotron XRD and environmental TEM assessment. Compare the temporal evolution of oxide scale thickness and phase transition onset between the experiments.
measurements: XRD peak shifts and appearance/disappearance of diffraction peaks over time
TEM imaging of oxide scale morphology and grain structure evolution
Kinetic data of oxide scale growth (e.g., thickness vs. time curves)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined in situ measurements do not resolve simultaneous, correlated changes in oxidation scale formation and phase transformations (i.e., if the temporal resolution or spatial correlation is no better than that achieved with separate methods), or if discrepancies arise that cannot be reconciled with established independent measurements, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
